transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. It’s nice to meet you too. Um, well, what finally pushed me to come in today... and honestly, I probably should have done this a while ago, but working as a health services manager, my schedule is just always so incredibly packed. But lately, things at the clinic have just been getting so frustrating for me, and I just can't ignore it anymore. 

A big part of my job is dealing with the data side of things, and we use EPIC for all our records, which is a beast of a system if you've ever dealt with it. So I'll sit down at my desk to start an EPIC quality report, or I'll go into one of our weekly clinic metrics meetings—and I always go in with every intention of tracking it. I really do. I have my coffee, my notes are open, I'm ready to dive in and look at the quarterly goals. But then, within just a few minutes, my mind has drifted so far off that I’m literally just rereading the exact same numbers on the screen over and over again. I'll read the same row of data five times and none of it actually computes. 

Or I’ll be sitting right there in the metrics meeting, looking right at the speaker, and I suddenly realize I completely missed the whole point of the discussion they just had for the last ten minutes. It’s like my brain just went on vacation without my permission. And it's embarrassing, frankly, because I've been doing this for years, I manage these people, and I should be able to sit through a standard administrative meeting without completely losing the thread of what my own team is talking about. It just takes so much energy to try and pull my focus back, and I'm just exhausted from pretending I'm catching everything when I'm really not.
Have you struggled with this kind of difficulty staying focused throughout your life, even going back to when you were a child, or is this a relatively new problem for you?

Well, no, it's definitely not a new thing, unfortunately. If I'm being completely honest, and looking back on it now, it’s been a theme my entire life, even way, way back when I was just a little girl in elementary school. I mean, I can still picture those old paper report cards my parents used to get. The teachers were always writing the exact same thing, year after year. They would say, you know, that I was a bright student, that I had a lot of potential, but that I was just so... careless. That was always the word they used: "careless." 

It used to drive my mother absolutely crazy. In fact, she literally had to sit right there next to me at the kitchen table every single night while I did my homework. And she couldn't just be in the room cooking or doing something else, she had to be right there, actively keeping me on task, because otherwise, I would just completely lose track of whatever assignment I was supposed to be doing. My mind would just wander off to a million other things. 

And, well, that's if I even had the materials to do the homework in the first place! Half the time, I'd get all the way home off the school bus and realize I had completely forgotten to bring my books home from school. They’d just be sitting there in my desk. It was just this constant, exhausting cycle for her, and for me, really, trying to keep all the pieces together. So, no, this isn't just something that started happening with the clinic metrics or as I got older. It’s always been there, just... taking different forms, I guess you could say.
Looking back at your childhood, would you say you were also physically restless, like having a hard time staying in your seat or feeling like you were driven by a motor?

You know, it's funny you ask that, because people always seem to assume that if you're struggling to pay attention, you must be bouncing off the walls, but no, not at all, actually. I was never the kid running around the classroom or climbing the furniture. I mean, I've seen kids like that—especially working in healthcare, you see the ones who literally cannot stay in a chair for more than three seconds—but me? No. I was physically very still. 

I would sit right there in my assigned seat, perfectly quiet, hands folded on my desk. And honestly, I think that was actually part of the problem, because since I wasn't causing a disruption or acting out, I just completely flew under the radar. I wasn't, you know, the stereotypical "bad kid" who couldn't sit down or was constantly interrupting the teacher. I would be sitting right at my desk, looking right at the chalkboard, but my mind was just... miles and miles away. 

I sometimes think about that, you know? Looking back on it now from an adult perspective. If I had been one of those kids who was jumping up and down or tapping their feet incessantly or driven by a motor like you said—which is a great way to put it, by the way—but if I had been visibly restless like that, maybe someone would have realized something was actually going on with me instead of just thinking I was a daydreamer or, like I said before, just careless. But physically, I was totally fine staying in my seat. I could sit there for hours. It was just that my brain wasn't in the seat with me, if that makes sense. I was perfectly content to just sit quietly and stare out the window at the playground or the trees, completely oblivious to the math lesson happening right in front of me. So the physical restlessness, the feeling like a motor is running... no, I've really never felt that way at all.
Growing up, did you often find yourself blurting out answers before a teacher finished a question, or struggling to wait your turn in games or conversations?

No, not really. I mean, I know exactly the type of behavior you're talking about—you know, the kids who just shout out the answer the second they know it, or honestly even if they don't know it, they just want to be heard. I've seen it with my own nieces and nephews, and even in some of the staff meetings I run now, there are always those people who just cannot wait their turn to speak and end up talking over everyone else. But for me, growing up, that really wasn't an issue at all. 

Like I was saying before, I was very quiet. Almost too quiet, really. I was definitely not the one raising my hand frantically or blurting things out. If anything, I was the complete opposite. I would be sitting there, and the teacher would ask a question, and even if by some miracle I had actually been paying attention and knew the answer, I would just sit there and wait for someone else to say it. I didn't want to draw attention to myself. And as for waiting my turn in games or things like that, I was always very patient. Well, maybe "patient" isn't the right word, but I was perfectly content to just wait. I'd be standing in line for four-square or whatever we were playing at recess, and I'd just be in my own little world, you know? Thinking about a book I was reading or what I was going to have for lunch, so the waiting never bothered me because I wasn't really focused on the game anyway. 

It’s interesting, really, because you hear all these things about kids who can't wait their turn or who interrupt constantly, and it just makes me think again about how different my experience was. I was just so internal with everything. The struggle was never about holding back what I wanted to say or do, it was just trying to stay connected to what was actually happening around me instead of floating off into my own thoughts. So, yeah, blurting things out or struggling to wait... that just wasn't me at all.
